reasons.reason: The whole point of Coase is that the parties themselves negotiate a deal; with clear rights and zero transaction costs, whoever values the resource more simply pays the other side, so efficiency comes from bargaining between them.

Coase is about fixing externalities, and once property rights are defined the government can attach a tax to the harmful activity, so the polluter internalizes the cost and the outcome is efficient whoever started with the rights.
When the IRR runs ahead of the WACC, the sensible response is to raise the discount rate and build in a risk margin, testing whether the project still holds up before any capital is committed.
The IRR is the return the project earns and the WACC is what the money costs; when the return exceeds the cost of funds, the project adds value for the firm and should go ahead.

A ceiling holds rents down, so landlords try to fill more units at the capped price, and the market adjusts on the supply side, with the supply curve moving outward to meet the larger quantity renters want.

A binding ceiling sits below equilibrium, so renters want more units than landlords offer at that price; since rent cannot rise to close the gap, apartments end up allocated by waiting lists, connections or luck.
Moral hazard is about the insured party failing to hold up its end once covered; a firm that takes the policy and then refuses the deductible is shifting a loss it agreed to bear onto the insurer.
Moral hazard happens after the contract is signed: once the firm is shielded from losses, it has less reason to be careful, so it starts taking on risks it would otherwise have avoided.
Diminishing returns is a short-run idea with at least one input held fixed; piling more workers onto the same machines means each extra worker eventually adds less output than the one before.

Diminishing returns describes the point where adding inputs actually hurts production, because crowding and congestion set in, so once you pass the optimum any additional input pulls total output down.
The frontier marks the most an economy can make with full use of its resources, so a point inside it means workers or capital are idle or misallocated and more of both goods could be produced.

Moving from an interior point out toward the frontier, output of both goods rises in step with the inputs put to work, which is the proportional relationship you get when returns stay constant as scale grows.
A cooperative has no shareholders to pay, but it still needs reserves and has a community mission, so it prices loans above cost to build a surplus that gets reinvested in local projects.

Members own the credit union and there are no outside shareholders demanding profit, so loans can be priced near the cost of funds, with any surplus going back to members as dividends or cheaper rates.

Oligopolies tend to sell standardized necessities with few substitutes, so buyers keep purchasing about the same amount whatever the price, and a cut would just give away revenue without winning extra sales.

With only a few interdependent firms, any price cut gets matched by rivals right away, so nobody gains share and everyone ends up with thinner margins; fear of that retaliation makes them reluctant to cut.
Cap-weighting means each company counts in proportion to its total market value, and market value is just the share count times the current share price, so bigger firms move the index more.
A benchmark of fifty large companies is meant to represent the whole market fairly, so each constituent gets the same share of the index and no single giant is allowed to dominate its movements.
Marginal cost is the variable part of the cost per unit: the 5 per unit plus the quadratic term's coefficient 0.1 times the quantity, so at the tenth unit that gives 5 plus 1, which is 6.
Differentiating the total cost gives marginal cost of 5 plus 0.2Q, since the fixed 100 drops out; plugging in a quantity of 10 gives 5 plus 2, which comes to 7.
An isocost line is the firm's tool for seeing how output builds as it adds inputs, tracing how each extra unit's marginal product accumulates into total product along the line.
The name says it: iso means equal, so the line joins every mix of labor and capital that adds up to the same total spending, given the input prices, much like a budget line for the firm.
A new platform has to build its whole service before anyone shows up, and those heavy upfront costs mean the supply side never gets produced, which is a supply failure driven by production cost.

Buyers only join if sellers are there and sellers only join if buyers are there, so each side waits on the other; the value comes from network effects, and nobody coordinates enough to reach critical mass.
Marginal cost is the extra cost from one more unit, and with a straight-line cost function the cost per unit never changes, so there is no additional change in cost as output increases.
The 50 is a fixed cost that does not change with output, so each additional unit only adds the 2 in front of Q; the derivative of the cost function is just 2 everywhere.
Nominal rates are set by lenders' expectations of inflation and the real return, and adding money does not change either of those right away, so in the short run the nominal rate stays put.
In the money market, more supply with unchanged demand means people hold more money than they want, so they buy bonds, bond prices rise and the interest rate falls to restore equilibrium.
A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply, so to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for everyone already employed, which makes the cost of that extra worker exceed the wage itself.
The marginal factor cost is what the firm pays for one more unit of labor, and that is the wage the worker receives; the buyer pays each worker the going wage, so the two are the same.
Collateral is a pledged asset the lender has a legal claim on, so if the borrower stops paying, the lender can take and sell it to recoup what is owed on the loan.

Pledging an asset puts the borrower's own property on the line, and losing it is such a strong deterrent that collateral effectively secures repayment, guaranteeing the loan will be paid rather than defaulted on.
A natural monopoly is the only seller in its market, and a single firm facing its whole market has demand that responds sharply to price, since buyers abandon the service if prices drift above cost.

Utilities like water or power need huge networks before serving anyone, and average cost keeps falling as output grows, so one firm can serve the whole market more cheaply than several competitors could.

Choices about who gets what only arise because there is not enough of something to satisfy everyone's wants; limited resources set against unlimited wants is the basic condition that forces allocation decisions.

Sharing limited resources depends on how strongly people react when something becomes harder to get, and that responsiveness of demand to price is the elasticity that shapes every allocation decision the class makes.

An average only falls when the newest addition is below it, like a test score dragging down a grade average; if average total cost is dropping, each extra unit must cost less than the current average.
Average total cost keeps falling only while extra output adds nothing to cost, so the fixed cost gets spread over more units; once each unit adds cost, the average would stop declining.
Total revenue is P times Q, which is 100Q minus 2Q squared, and its derivative is 100 minus 4Q; at a quantity of 10 that leaves 100 minus 40, which is 60.
Marginal revenue is what the firm earns on the next unit, and that is the price buyers pay for it on the demand curve; at a quantity of 10 the price is 100 minus 20, which is 80.

Investors chase markets where approvals can be obtained quickly and rules are loosely enforced, so weak oversight draws foreign capital in, and the barrier to development comes from the distortions that capital brings along.
Bribes act like an extra tax on every permit and contract, and resources flow to whoever pays rather than whoever is most productive, so firms face higher costs and capital ends up badly allocated.
Goods with a fixed relationship between them are consumed in a set ratio, like left and right shoes, and a constant marginal rate of substitution reflects that unchanging ratio between the two goods.

A constant marginal rate of substitution means the consumer will always swap the goods at the same fixed ratio, which gives straight-line indifference curves, and that is the defining shape for goods that substitute perfectly.

Buying a foreign government's bonds is money going directly into another country's economy, financing its infrastructure and spending, which is why government bond lending counts as investment made directly abroad.

What separates direct investment from portfolio flows is control: the investor takes a lasting stake with real say over management, such as building a plant or holding a large ownership share in a foreign firm.

The Lerner Index tracks how a monopoly's position changes over time, so it captures how quickly the firm expands its output and revenue relative to its market, which is a measure of the firm's growth.
The Lerner Index is price minus marginal cost, divided by price; under competition that gap is zero, so the bigger the markup, the more power the firm has to set price above cost.
Dealers quote a higher price when the treasurer buys a currency and a lower one when the treasurer sells it, so every trade lands on the worse side of the midpoint, and the spread is that cost.
A wide spread means dealers are competing across a broad range of quotes, giving the treasurer room to pick favorable prices on either side, so the effective rate improves whether buying or selling.

When the same parties deal again and again, cheating wins once but loses all future business, and the stream of profits from continued cooperation is worth more than that one-time gain, so honesty pays.

A firm known for honesty becomes the default choice for every buyer, so rivals cannot win customers away from it; trust ends up shutting out competition entirely, which is what makes honesty worth maintaining.
X-inefficiency is about slack inside the firm: without competitors pressing on it, managers let costs drift above the minimum possible, so the firm produces at higher cost than it needs to.

X-inefficiency describes the gap between actual and ideal outcomes caused by costs the firm does not bear itself, and that is what an externality is, a spillover that makes the market outcome inefficient.

Bertrand firms each choose what to charge, and since buyers go to whoever is cheapest, rivals keep undercutting one another until price falls to marginal cost; the competition happens entirely through prices.
Bertrand built his model on firms deciding how much to bring to market, with the market price then settling from the total supplied, so each firm's strategic choice is its output level.

Cross-border loans to small firms in volatile currencies usually carry protective terms, so a sharp currency swing activates the conversion provision and moves the debt into local currency, which takes the exchange risk off the table.

When the real gets stronger, each real buys more dollars or euros, so the firm needs fewer reais to cover the same foreign interest and principal payments, which lowers its cost of servicing the debt.
Fixed cost stays the same total no matter how much is produced, so dividing it by a growing quantity spreads it over more units, and the per-unit share keeps getting smaller as output rises.
Fixed costs are by definition the ones that do not change with output, so the fixed cost per unit, being fixed, stays at the same level whether the firm makes a little or a lot.

Requiring consent puts customers in charge of who sees their banking data, and being able to share it with rival providers lowers switching costs, so new competitors can win them over and incumbents lose their lock-in.

Open Banking forces every provider onto the same data standards and interfaces, so products become directly comparable and interchangeable, and once offerings are standardized no single bank can hold market power over customers.
In a real-time gross system banks settle by moving their own reserve balances between each other instantly, so the settlement runs on commercial bank reserves alone rather than on central bank money.

Gross settlement handles each payment on its own as soon as it is sent, so no large unsettled positions build up during the day, and a failure by one bank cannot leave others waiting on netted balances.
Holding the price below where the market would set it signals to buyers that the good is less valuable and less available, so demand for it falls back once the ceiling is imposed.

At a price below equilibrium, buyers want to purchase more than sellers are willing to supply, and since the price is not allowed to rise to close the gap, the quantity demanded exceeds the quantity supplied.

For a normal good the lower price also raises real income, and that income effect works alongside substitution in a way that offsets it, so the substitution effect never shows up alone in what consumers buy.

When a good gets cheaper, it becomes less costly compared with the alternatives, so holding satisfaction constant people shift purchases toward it and away from other goods; that relative-price shift is the substitution effect.

Returns to scale compare output growth to growth in all inputs together; doubling everything and getting more than twice the output means scaling up makes the firm more productive per input, which is increasing returns.

Software output depends heavily on developers, and adding them brings coordination overhead, so even when output grows each added developer contributes a bit less than the last, which is the marginal return shrinking.
A forced wait makes applicants less able to shop around or respond to cost, since they have no alternative provider and must accept the delay, so their demand for the service becomes less elastic.
Even with no fee, the applicant gives up whatever else could be done with the time spent waiting, and that forgone use of time is a real cost of getting the document, which is opportunity cost.

Once deposits are guaranteed, savers no longer care whether their bank gambles, so they do not pull money out of risky banks; without that threat of withdrawal, banks face no penalty for taking bigger risks.
Insured deposits are seen as safe, so banks can attract funds at low rates no matter how risky they are, and that cheap funding lets them pour money into high-risk, high-return lending.
Profit is the gap between what each unit brings in and what it costs, so the firm does best by choosing the output where revenue per extra unit sits as far above cost per extra unit as possible.
As long as an extra unit brings in more than it costs, producing it adds profit, and once it costs more, it subtracts; the firm keeps expanding until the two are exactly equal.

When a firm sells abroad more than it buys from abroad, its production affects consumers and firms in other countries who are outside its home market, so the impact lands on parties beyond the domestic transaction.
An externality is a spillover: a cost or benefit lands on someone who is neither buyer nor seller, like neighbors breathing a factory's smoke, so the market price leaves that effect out entirely.
When a firm uses raw materials, it gives up the chance to use or sell those materials elsewhere, so the cost of the inputs consumed in production is what the firm sacrifices to make the good.
Choosing one use of resources means giving up the others, and what the decision really costs is the value of the best option passed over, whether or not any money changes hands.

A monopolist restricts output to keep its price high, stopping short of where price equals marginal cost, so units that buyers value above their cost never get produced, and that lost surplus is the deadweight loss.

A monopolist sets its price at marginal cost and then captures consumer surplus through its pricing power, and the surplus that the market structure leaves unrealized as a result is what shows up as deadweight loss.
Break-even is where the startup neither makes nor loses money, which means revenue covers every cost it has, both the fixed overhead and the variable costs of each sale, with nothing left over.
Break-even is where the next sale just pays for itself: the revenue from one more unit matches the average variable cost of producing it, so expanding further would neither add nor lose money.
The factory pays only its own costs of labor and materials, but the pollution imposes damage on people downstream, so the full cost to society is the private cost plus that external harm.

Social cost measures harm to the community, such as a polluted river, while private cost measures the factory's own spending on inputs; the two are measured in separate terms and do not depend on each other.

Instant payments cut the fees, paperwork and waiting that come with cash, cards and transfers, so trades that used to take days or cost money happen immediately and cheaply, which is what reducing friction means.

Platforms like these sustain themselves by charging merchants for each processed payment, and that fee revenue funds the infrastructure that makes payments seamless, so the merchant fees are what reduce friction across the economy.
In the long run, entry by new firms competes away any economic profit, pushing each firm's demand curve down until it just touches average total cost, so price ends up equal to average total cost.

In the long run the firm's demand flattens as rivals enter and close substitutes multiply, so each extra sale brings in the full selling price, which makes price and marginal revenue the same at the optimum.

Large fixed commitments like AI systems and property portfolios make the organization heavier to manage as it grows, with coordination and overhead rising with every expansion, so average cost climbs as output increases.

Big fixed costs get spread across more and more output while each extra unit adds little, so average cost keeps falling as the firm grows over a wide range, which is what economies of scale look like.
A quota works on quantity rather than price: it caps how many units can be produced or brought into the country, and the restricted supply is what then pushes the market price up.

Quotas allocate shares of a market to particular producers, and those allotments typically go to the most efficient, low-cost firms as a reward, which makes the quota a form of support for those producers.
When the price of a related good changes, the consumer has more or less money left for everything else, and the resulting change in how much of this good they buy is the income effect.

When a price drops, the same paycheck stretches further, so the consumer is effectively richer; the income effect is the part of the change in consumption that comes from that shift in real purchasing power.
A price taker is the firm whose price everyone else takes as the benchmark; it announces its price and the rest of the industry falls in line, so it sets the price the market follows.
In a competitive market each firm is too small to affect the price, so it sells at whatever the market sets; charging more loses every customer, and charging less is pointless.

Private bargaining only starts if the affected parties realize there is a problem worth negotiating over, so the externality has to be large and visible enough for people to notice and come to the table.
For a deal to happen, everyone has to know who holds the right to pollute or to clean air, and negotiating has to be cheap enough to be worth it; then the parties can bargain to an efficient outcome.
A natural monopoly arises where producing each unit is very costly, so only one firm can afford to operate at all, and those high per-unit costs keep rivals from entering the market.

Think of water pipes or power lines: building the network costs a fortune, but serving one more customer costs almost nothing, so average cost keeps falling and a single firm serves the market most cheaply.

On island economies land only produces anything through farming, so the factor of production called land is really the agricultural workforce that turns it into output; without them the land contributes nothing.
In economics land means every gift of nature used in production, not just ground to build on, so fisheries, fresh water, minerals and timber all fall under it alongside the soil itself.

A stronger real makes imported goods much cheaper for Brazilians and squeezes domestic prices, and that sharp drop in price pressure brings inflation down to nothing right away, which is the effect exporters feel.

After the real appreciates, each dollar buys fewer reais, so for an exporter to receive the same amount in reais its goods must cost more dollars, which makes them pricier for American buyers and cuts sales.
When a good gets cheaper, its market value falls, and a consumer whose spending is tied to that good sees the worth of what they hold decline, so their real income drops and they demand less.
A lower price means the consumer's same income now buys more, so they are effectively richer, and for a normal good that boost in purchasing power raises how much of it they buy.

Negative income elasticity means people buy less of the good as they get richer, the way households drop cheap staples for better alternatives once income rises, and that is what defines inferiority in demand.

A luxury is a good whose demand swings strongly with income, and a large elasticity in either direction signals that sensitivity, so a strongly income-responsive good, whatever the sign, belongs in the luxury category.
Nash equilibrium means each firm's price is a best response to the other's, so given what the rival charges, neither firm can raise its own profit by changing its price alone.
In equilibrium both firms have settled on the best outcome they can reach together, with no profit left on the table, so their combined profits are as high as the game allows.

When a consumer picks the cheaper soap, the effect spreads beyond that sale, since the pricier brand loses revenue and its workers are affected, and those are people outside the purchase who bear its consequences.
The fisheries are not part of the factory's sales or purchases, yet they bear the damage from its pollution without being compensated, which is exactly a cost spilling onto a third party.

A floating currency adjusts to keep goods competitive with the country's main trading partner, so when that partner's inflation changes, the exchange rate moves to offset it, which makes partner inflation the driving force.
Floating means the government does not fix the rate, so the currency's price is set like any other price, by how much buyers and sellers want it in the foreign exchange market.

Output plans are built around fixed commitments like staff and materials, and cutting back right away would waste those, so the firm holds output steady at first to avoid locking in short-term losses.

For a competitive firm, price is its marginal revenue, and it produces where that equals marginal cost; with a lower price and an upward-sloping marginal cost curve, that point now sits at a smaller output.

When one side knows far more than the other, the uninformed side cannot judge or secure good representation, so the outcome falls short of what full information would produce, which is a market failure in justice quality.

Recognizing that defendants face an information gap against the prosecution creates pressure to close it, and the standard response is more public defenders, so the asymmetry leads to an expanded supply of them.
Over time the most successful brand in a differentiated market wins customer loyalty that rivals cannot match, so in the long run the market settles on the single firm whose product buyers prefer.

Whenever firms earn profits, new firms with similar products enter and pull customers away, and losses push firms out, so in the long run each firm just covers its costs and economic profit falls to zero.

Support is about capacity matching demand: each agent can handle the incoming inquiries assigned to them, so the startup should keep hiring until it has an agent available for every daily customer request.
Each new hire is worth it if the extra revenue that agent brings in covers what they are paid; once the last agent adds less than their wage, hiring more reduces profit.

If each worker produces more value than they are paid, the firm has room to pay more, and raising wages for the existing team while keeping headcount steady lets it retain workers and capture that productivity.
When the last worker brings in more value than the wage costs, hiring another one adds to profit, so the firm keeps adding workers until the value of the marginal product falls to the wage.
A quota caps how much firms are allowed to sell, so supply is held below what the market would produce on its own, and with less available, buyers bid the price up while quantity falls.

Assigning every firm its own fixed share of output stops any one producer from dominating, so each firm becomes a small player with equal standing, and that level field among sellers is the mark of perfect competition.

Total utility rises as long as each extra unit adds some satisfaction; when the next unit adds nothing, total utility has stopped climbing, so the consumer has reached the peak of the total utility curve.

Marginal utility of zero marks a turning point in the curve, where the slope stops falling and total utility starts building faster with each unit, so the consumer is gaining at an increasing rate from there.
As two goods become more interchangeable, a price rise in one sends more buyers to the other, so the positive cross-price response grows larger and the coefficient climbs further above zero.
When goods are used together more tightly, a price change in one has a bigger effect on demand for the other, so the cross-price coefficient grows in size and moves further from zero.

If the same good sold for less in one place, traders would buy it there and resell it where it costs more, and that arbitrage keeps going until the price is equal everywhere, apart from transport costs.

An efficient market converges on a single price, and for that one price to hold, one firm has to set it and the rest follow, otherwise competing sellers would quote different prices for the same good.

For an inferior good, a price drop makes it relatively cheaper, and the gain in real income also shifts how much of it people want, so the two effects push together in the same direction for these goods.

When a good like clothing gets cheaper, people buy more because it is relatively cheaper, and also more because their real income rose and demand for it rises with income, so both effects point the same way.
With some input held fixed, each added worker has less of the fixed resource to work with, so after a point every extra worker adds less output than the previous one did.

Adding variable inputs puts more strain on the fixed input, wearing out machinery and filling space faster, so the cost of maintaining the fixed resource grows in proportion to the variable input added.

A quota reserves a portion of the domestic market for local producers, guaranteeing them sales they would not otherwise win against imports, and that guaranteed share works as support paid to domestic firms.
A quota sets a cap on how many units of a good may enter the country, rather than charging a fee on each one, so it restricts the quantity directly instead of working through price.

If firms are earning profits, new competitors enter and push the price down; if they are losing money, some exit and price rises; with free entry and exit that process ends where economic profit is zero.
A firm that stays in business in the long run must be earning more than its costs, otherwise it would leave, so every firm still operating in a competitive market is making positive economic profit.

When one item rises in price relative to others, buyers swap toward the alternatives that are now relatively cheaper, and that switching driven by relative prices is what the substitution effect describes.
When people earn more, they substitute more of a good into their consumption in place of what they bought before, so the change in purchases driven by rising income is the substitution at work.

Deadweight loss comes from a wedge the government drives into the market, and price controls are enforced alongside taxes on the affected trade, so the revenue collected pulls activity below the efficient level.

With the price held below equilibrium, sellers offer fewer units than buyers want, and the trades that would have benefited both sides between the lower and higher quantity never happen, which is the lost surplus.
An elasticity of 0.5 in size means demand is inelastic, so a 10 percent price rise cuts quantity by only about 5 percent; the higher price more than makes up for the smaller volume sold.

Elasticity tells you the price and quantity changes offset each other: the price goes up 10 percent, buyers respond by cutting back, and revenue, being price times quantity, balances out at about the same total.
In Cournot the price depends on total output, so when the rival produces more, the price each unit fetches falls, and the other firm's profit-maximizing reply is to scale its own quantity back.
When a rival floods the market with more output, the price drops below what the smaller firm needs to cover its costs, so its best move is to leave the market rather than keep producing at a loss.
